findings.rationale: readClaims() base64-decodes and JSON.parses the JWT payload without ever verifying the token signature. Any attacker who can influence the stored token can craft an unsigned/forged payload (e.g. {"role":"admin"}) and have it accepted as authentic claims.

The admin authorization decision is made purely from self-asserted, unverified JWT claims (role field). No signature check, no issuer/audience check, so role escalation is trivial if the token can be tampered with.
The exp claim is parsed but never validated, so an expired token still grants admin access — sessions effectively never expire for authorization checks.

No validation that the token actually contains three dot-separated segments or valid base64/JSON; a malformed token causes an unhandled exception in the route guard, which can break navigation (DoS of the app) rather than failing closed cleanly.

Access control is enforced only client-side in the route guard based on a locally decoded token; without corresponding server-side authorization this check can be bypassed by manipulating client state.

readClaims() base64-decodes and JSON.parses the JWT payload without ever verifying the token's signature or issuer/audience. Any attacker-crafted or tampered token (e.g. one whose payload was re-encoded with "role":"admin") is accepted as authentic, so all claims used downstream are untrusted attacker-controlled data.

The route guard makes the admin authorization decision solely from unverified client-side claims (claims.role === 'admin' and claims.exp). A user can set an arbitrary token in TokenStore or modify the unsigned payload to gain admin routes; authorization must be re-enforced and signature-validated server-side.

No validation that the token contains three dot-separated segments or that the payload is valid base64/JSON; a malformed token causes an uncaught TypeError/SyntaxError that propagates out of the CanActivate guard, breaking navigation (availability/error-handling issue).

readClaims() base64-decodes and JSON.parses the JWT payload without ever verifying the token signature. Any claim read this way (role, sub, exp) is attacker-controlled, since the token is only stored client-side and can be replaced with a hand-crafted unsigned token. It must not be used for any trust decision.

The guard makes its expiry/authorization pre-check from unverified, user-controllable JWT claims (claims.exp). A forged token with a far-future exp bypasses this check; if the backend /api/session ever trusts the presented bearer token loosely, the client-side decode provides no security. Expiry/role must be validated server-side against a signature-verified token.

A malformed token (no '.' segment, non-base64 payload, or non-JSON payload) makes token.split('.')[1] undefined or atob/JSON.parse throw. The exception propagates out of readClaims into adminGuard (line 15), which has no try/catch, causing an unhandled error in the router activation path instead of a clean deny.

claims.exp is used without validating that it is a number; if the claim is missing, NaN*1000 < Date.now() evaluates to false, so the token is treated as non-expired and the guard continues rather than denying access.
